content.content: Topic: why the number of subsets of an n-element set doubles each time n grows by one

input.message:
Why the Number of Subsets Doubles

Take any finite set with n elements. It has many subsets: the empty set, the whole set, and every combination in between. The count is 2^n, and the reason it doubles each time one element is added shows what a subset really is.

A subset is completely described by a list of yes-or-no decisions. For each element, ask whether it belongs to the subset. Each element offers two choices, and the choices are independent, so n elements give n binary decisions and the number of distinct outcomes is 2 multiplied by itself n times. The multiplication principle already explains the formula. The doubling claim asks for something more local: why does going from n to n+1 multiply the count by exactly two, rather than adding some amount?

Let A be a set with n elements, and let B be A with one extra element x. Sort the subsets of B into two groups that do not overlap: those that contain x and those that do not.

The subsets that do not contain x are exactly the subsets of A. Suppose A has N subsets. Then this group has N members.

The subsets that contain x can be matched one-to-one with the first group. Given any subset S of A, the set S together with x is a subset of B that contains x, and removing x from it returns S. So the map S to S-with-x is a bijection, and this group also has N members.

The total is N + N = 2N. The new element does not disturb the old subsets. It gives each of them a twin, one with x and one without. Nothing about the old subsets changes, and no subset is counted twice, because the presence or absence of x tells the twins apart. That is the whole mechanism of doubling.

A concrete check helps. Start with A = {a}, which has two subsets: the empty set and {a}. Add b. The subsets of {a, b} are the empty set, {a}, {b}, and {a, b}, four in all. Each earlier subset appears once without b and once with it. Adding c gives eight subsets, and so on.
